Eye of a Needle
EYE uv uh NEE-dul
n. (our Lord's figure for the impossibility of a rich man saving himself)
Greek trupema rhaphidos in Matthew, trumalia rhaphidos in Mark, the hole or perforation of a sewing needle; Luke has trumalias belones, a surgeon's needle. Named in all three synoptic Gospels.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The eye of a needle is our Lord's measure of impossibility, spoken immediately after the rich young ruler went away sorrowful: “And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24). Mark repeats it in the same words and Luke gives it with a surgeon's needle, the finest then known. The disciples understood it exactly as it sounds — they were exceedingly amazed and asked who then can be saved — and our Lord did not soften it. He answered that with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible, which is the point of the saying and the reason it must not be blunted. The popular explanation that the Needle's Eye was a small gate in Jerusalem through which a camel could pass on its knees has no ancient evidence whatever and first appears many centuries later; it was invented to make the camel merely difficult instead of impossible. That ruins the doctrine. Our Lord chose the largest beast in Palestine and the smallest hole in common use because He meant a thing that cannot be done, and then located the possibility in God alone. Salvation is not hard for the rich. It is impossible for anyone, and God does it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Eye of a needle, the perforation of a sewing needle; used by Christ as a figure of absolute impossibility, a camel being the largest beast and the needle's eye the smallest opening.

Greek trupema rhaphidos, the hole of a needle, Matthew 19:24.

Greek trumalia rhaphidos in Mark 10:25.

Luke has trumalias belones, the eye of a surgeon's needle, Luke 18:25.

Spoken after the departure of the rich young ruler.

Answered by With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible, Matthew 19:26.

Key Scripture

Mat 19:24 — "And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God."

Mar 10:25 — "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God."

Luk 18:25 — "For it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God."

Mat 19:26 — "But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible."

Modern Corruption

The saying is defused by a legend about a camel gate, turning an impossibility into an inconvenience and emptying the answer our Lord gave.

expand to see more

The most persistent corruption of this text is the pulpit tradition that the eye of the needle was a low postern gate in the Jerusalem wall, so that a camel could squeeze through by being unloaded and made to kneel — from which preachers draw a lesson about humility and letting go of possessions. There is no evidence for such a gate in any ancient source, and the explanation is not attested until long after the New Testament era. It is an invention, and its effect is to replace an impossibility with a difficulty, which is precisely the move the disciples did not make and our Lord did not permit.

The second corruption, from the opposite direction, is the ascetic reading that makes wealth itself damning and poverty meritorious, as though the camel could pass by being poor. Our Lord says the impossibility is general: the disciples ask who then can be saved, not which rich man. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathaea were wealthy men and are not in hell. What damns is trust in riches, and the remedy is not redistribution but regeneration, which only God performs.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek trupema or trumalia rhaphidos, the hole of a needle; our Lord's figure of sheer impossibility.

expand to see more

Greek rhaphis, a needle, from rhapto, to sew.

Greek trupema, a hole, a perforation; trumalia, an aperture.

Luke uses belone, a surgeon's or fine needle.

The camel was the largest beast commonly known in Palestine.

Named in Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25 and Luke 18:25.
